args.question: How do swarms choose a place to settle or build a new nest, and what site conditions do they prefer?

steps.observation:
Natural swarming of bees and how to prevent it [microform]
(page 1 of the scan) There is nothing on the farm which requires so little care, in proportion to the returns, as bees. This is why they ave sometimes kept at a loss: because the care they need is comparatively small and is often neglected. ‘They require less attention than some other things; but what they do require they must have. The management of an apiary for honey must be approached in the same business like manner as, for example, the management of a dairy herd for milk. ‘There is no more “luck” or “chance” in the one than in the other. Scientific methods govern both. Failure in either is due to some definite cause which must be dis- covered and mastered before success can be attained.

(page 10 of the scan) For Comb Honey Production the work in the supers has to be so crowded to get well-filled sections that it is practically impossible to keep the bees from con- tracting the swarming impulse. In fact the best work in comb honey supers is usually done by first swarms newly hived on starters. They are full of energy due to the completely changed conditions, they have no brood to care for and having narrow foundation starters instead of full sheets or combs in the brood chamber they throw their working force strongly into the supers.

steps.answer: The sources I searched don't directly answer how honeybees choose a new nest site. The catalog has no subject heading for nest-site selection or swarm settling, and the 1915 swarming text I read (Natural swarming of bees and how to prevent it, p. 1 and p. 10) covers general apiary management and how first swarms behave in comb-honey supers, not where swarms settle. Older beekeeping books that might discuss swarm settling include The bee-keeper's text-book (1867) and The Bee-keeper's Manual (1860), but I did not read them. Any pre-1929 account would also predate modern research on scout bees and nest-cavity evaluation, so treat it as historical. For a current answer, a reference librarian could look for recent entertainment of the topic in the catalog under Honeybee--Behavior or Swarming.
